science.title: A diet containing Moringa oleifera alters the goat rumen microbiome and improves animal performance: an insight into bacteria, ciliates and rumen anaerobic fungi
science.description: In the present study, we investigated the impact of Moringa oleifera feed on rumen and fecal microbial communities, including bacteria, ciliates, and anaerobic fungi in lactating goats (Capra hircus). The goats were divided into three groups based on dietary regimes: masoor straw (MS, n = 10), 20% moringa leaf meal (20% MLM, n = 10), and 30% moringa leaf meal (30% MLM, n = 10), and were maintained on this diet for 180 days. Animal performance parameters, daily feed and nutrients intake, fortnightly milk yield and body weight changes, and feed digestibility were measured. Rumen digesta and fecal samples were collected at the end of the experiment, and amplicon sequencing targeting the 16 S rRNA, ciliates-specific 18 S rRNA, and rumen anaerobic fungi-specific ITS1 genes were carried out. Moringa-fed goats showed improved nutrient utilization efficiency, body weight gain (BWG), and milk production. Linear mixed-effect model analysis demonstrated that milk yield increased significantly from third fortnight onwards in both moringa -supplemented groups. In the rumen solid and liquid fractions, a moringa diet increased the Bacillota: Bacteroidota ratio, which could be associated with lower residual feed intake, improved metabolism, and thus better body weight gain and milk yield. An increase in the proteolytic bacterial phylum Pseudomonadota was observed with the moringa diet, which could be linked with high protein content in the moringa and the diet containing it. In the rumen solid fraction, several plant carbohydrate degraders and fermenters such as Coprococcus, Ruminococcus, Succinimonas, Mediterraneibacter, Cellulosilyticum, Butyricicoccus, Cellulosibacter, Ruminobacter, Saccharofermentans, Agathobacter were significantly abundant in the moringa-fed group (Kruskal-Wallis, Dunn’s post hoc test, adjusted p ≤ 0.05). Ciliates like Enoploplastron, Metadinium and Diploplastron significantly increased (Kruskal-Wallis, Dunn’s post hoc test, adjusted p ≤ 0.05), while Entodinium was reduced in the rumen digesta samples of moringa feed groups. The fibre-degrading fungal genus Neocallimastix was less abundant in the rumen of the goats fed with moringa. Overall, these findings suggest that moringa supplementation positively influences feed digestion, nutrient intake, body weight gain, and milk yield, possibly through modulating rumen microbial communities in the lactating goats. These findings also highlight the complex interactions between moringa-based diet and rumen microbes, which may further improve goat health and milk production. However, future experiments focusing on the analysis of phytochemical composition of moringa leaves and rumen fermentation parameters would further strengthen these findings.

science.title: Network-based gene prioritization using hybrid scoring for complex disease module discovery
science.description: Complex diseases arise from perturbations in interconnected biological networks rather than isolated genetic defects. Network-based approaches provide a systematic framework for understanding disease mechanisms through protein-protein interaction data, yet most existing methods are developed and validated on a single disease or pathogenic mechanism, leaving their generalizability largely untested. We present a disease-agnostic computational framework that integrates five biological databases to construct robust ground truth gene sets, applies sensitivity analysis to identify high-confidence disease genes, and combines network topology with diffusion algorithms for systematic gene prioritization, requiring only a disease name as input. Our approach employs a noisy-OR fusion strategy to integrate evidence from DISEASES, GeneCards, OpenTargets, Gene2Phenotype, and NCBI Gene, followed by genetic algorithm optimization and random walk with restart for gene prioritization. Disease-relevant subnetworks were extracted and analyzed using complementary clustering algorithms (Leiden and MCL) to identify modules validated through pathway enrichment analysis. Without disease-specific tuning, the same workflow was applied unchanged to two neurodegenerative disorders and one autoimmune disease, chosen to span markedly different pathogenic mechanisms: Alzheimer disease (AD), Parkinson disease (PD), and rheumatoid arthritis (RA). In each case the framework recovered known disease genes and identified biologically coherent, disease-specific modules: in AD, 17 stable high-confidence genes and modules enriched in lipid and cholesterol metabolism and amyloid precursor protein processing; in PD, 17 stable genes and modules associated with mitophagy, ubiquitin-proteasome signaling, and mitochondrial dysfunction; in RA, 20 stable genes and modules enriched in antigen presentation and JAK-STAT cytokine signaling. This consistent recovery of mechanistically distinct, biologically appropriate signatures from a single unmodified pipeline demonstrates that the framework generalizes across disease categories rather than being tuned to any one of them. By prioritizing biological validation through pathway enrichment over predictive accuracy, and by demonstrating consistent performance across neurodegenerative and autoimmune contexts without disease-specific adaptation, the framework offers a versatile, readily extensible tool for exploratory analyses of disease mechanisms, including diseases for which prior mechanistic knowledge is limited. All code, data, and results are publicly available to ensure reproducibility.
